plain: This asks whether the state should be able to override local zoning to allow more housing. Colorado did so in 2024 with laws on backyard homes, housing near transit, parking and who can share a home.

short_version.text: Colorado already overrode local zoning in 2024 to allow backyard homes and denser housing near transit. Prices and rents are high and easing only slightly. Zoning is one cost among several, and it isn't yet clear how much housing the new laws will add. The trade-off is more homes against local control.

agree_means: Agreeing supports state laws that override local zoning to allow more housing, like Colorado’s 2024 laws on backyard homes, density near transit and occupancy limits.
disagree_means: Disagreeing leaves zoning decisions to cities and counties and opposes the 2024 state laws.

example.text: In a city covered by the 2024 laws, a homeowner can now add a backyard home that local rules may have banned. Residents who wanted larger-lot neighborhoods lose some say over that.

now.text: Local rules are restrictive. A statewide study found zoning bans most duplexes, townhouses and apartments across Colorado. The National Zoning Atlas says Colorado has the fifth highest home prices and third highest rent in the nation.

sources.quote: Local zoning codes in Colorado overwhelmingly prohibit duplexes, townhouses, condominiums and apartment units, as well as single-family homes on small lots, effectively outlawing the types of housing that real estate experts say are most affordable to build.

sources.title: Nearly 70% of Colorado land zoned for housing prohibits the most affordable types of homes, study finds (The Colorado Sun)

now.text: Some residents are pushing back. Lakewood voters repealed new zoning in April 2026, and Littleton voters wrote single-family zoning into its charter in 2025. Lawmakers dropped small-lot bills in 2026.

sources.title: Lakewood voters strike down pro-density zoning as repeal campaign dominates (The Colorado Sun, via Denverite)
sources.quote: Lakewood voters decisively repealed the city’s new zoning laws on Tuesday night, striking down a change that would have allowed more duplexes, triplexes and other multi-unit housing across the city’s suburban neighborhoods.

sources.title: Littleton Ballot Question 3A: Voters approve new restrictions on homebuilding (The Colorado Sun)
sources.quote: Littleton voters Tuesday night approved a ballot measure enshrining single-family zoning in the city’s charter, effectively blocking local officials from allowing denser forms of housing across most of the southern Denver suburb.

stakes.text: The state’s climate plan says housing type and location affect pollution. Townhouses and apartments use less energy than detached homes, and homes near transit shorten trips. They say outward growth adds driving, uses more water and open land, and raises wildfire risk.

research_notes: Method: the Colorado Department of Local Affairs pages return 403 to clients without a browser user agent, so I confirmed those quotes in the browser (marked via: browser). All other pages were fetched directly and every quote was checked against the fetched text. The Colorado legislature's own bill pages returned an error to automated fetches, so the 2024 laws are described from the Colorado Department of Local Affairs pages (ADU law HB24-1152, transit law HB24-1313) and the Colorado Sun's May 2024 summary (HB24-1007 on unrelated occupants was signed April 2024; HB24-1304 on parking was not used). The Sun's description of a 40-units-per-acre standard was left out because the state agency describes the final transit law as a formula-based goal. The shared web-search budget ran out mid-task. Not found: any measured effect of the 2024 laws on rents or prices, or a count of backyard homes permitted since the law took effect. The Sun credits falling Denver rents to a wave of new apartments, not to the 2024 laws. No home-rule legal analysis was found. Double-check: the Sun's 2024 article was written before the governor signed every bill, so details of HB24-1313 and HB24-1152 come from DOLA's current pages where possible. The $35 million incentive figure is from that 2024 article. The National Zoning Atlas figures were updated by the researchers in Sept 2025 for lot sizes (not used here). The Roadmap 2.0 environmental points are a state agency plan. Dates marked accessed have no publication date.
